query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A controlled surface engineering treatment that promotes in situ oxidation on a Cr-containing high‐entropy alloy (such as AlCoCrFeNi) will form a Cr-rich, dual-phase passive layer that enhances tribo‐corrosion resistance under high-temperature conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk Cr-containing high‐entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi) with its native microstructure and oxidation behavior.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled surface treatment (e.g., in situ oxidation or deposition of an engineered coating) designed to create a gradient Cr-rich passive layer with a dual-phase structure and enhanced surface hardness.
generation.conditions: Exposure to elevated temperatures (e.g., 450–650 °C) combined with simultaneous tribological wear and corrosive environments (such as molten salt or aggressive electrolyte exposures).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a Cr-rich passive surface layer exhibiting a dual-phase microstructure with a gradient in composition and increased hardness at the top surface.
generation.mechanism: The engineered surface layer is expected to promote the development of a protective, self-healing oxide scale that resists further oxidation and suppresses the synergistic effects of wear and corrosion. The hard, gradient layer reduces mechanical damage while the enriched Cr content facilitates formation of corrosion‐resistant oxides, mitigating accelerated degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy should exhibit a lower degradation rate (e.g., reduced weight loss and less surface damage) under high-temperature tribo‐corrosion conditions compared to the untreated alloy.
generation.baseline: Untreated Cr-containing AlCoCrFeNi alloy, which lacks the engineered surface layer and consequently shows higher rates of degradation under combined high-temperature, tribological, and corrosive conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement may be limited if the mechanical demands (e.g., extreme abrasion) exceed the durability of the engineered layer, or if prolonged exposure leads to degradation of the passive film. Additionally, scale-up and uniformity of the surface treatment might affect the overall performance.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvement in tribo‐corrosion resistance is uncertain and may vary with specific processing conditions, environmental parameters, and treatment durability over long-term service.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens: one group of the base Cr-containing HEA (AlCoCrFeNi) without any surface treatment and one group treated with the controlled surface engineering process to create the Cr-rich passive layer. Expose both sets to a combined high-temperature (450–650 °C) environment with simultaneous mechanical wear (e.g., via a tribometer setup) and corrosive medium (such as molten salt or saline solution) for a fixed duration. Post-exposure, evaluate the weight loss, surface morphology, microhardness profiles, and phase compositions.
measurements: Surface and cross-sectional microstructure via SEM/TEM
Microhardness distribution at the treated layer
Oxide scale composition (e.g., via EDS or XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction in degradation (e.g., similar weight loss, surface damage, and mechanical deterioration) compared to the untreated specimens under identical conditions, then the hypothesis that the engineered Cr-rich passive layer enhances tribo-corrosion resistance will be falsified.

The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe. decision.trend: Earlier HEA research has focused on optimizing bulk compositions and processing routes (e.g., arc melting, spark plasma sintering, selective laser melting, and magnetron sputtering) to achieve stable single-phase microstructures with enhanced mechanical properties, oxidation resistance, and corrosion behavior at high temperatures. Several studies have harnessed Cr and other refractory elements to promote the formation of protective oxides and improve high-temperature durability. While these strategies have successfully addressed aspects such as strength, ductility, oxidation and radiation resistance, they have not yet fully tackled the combined problem of tribological wear with corrosive degradation under high-temperature conditions.
decision.unsolved: The integrated challenge of tribo‐corrosion — where wear and corrosion synergistically accelerate degradation — persists. Specifically, there is a need for a material system that not only forms protective oxide scales in harsh, high-temperature environments but also exhibits a surface microstructure capable of resisting mechanical abrasion.
decision.lever: Implement controlled surface treatments (such as in situ oxidation or deposition of engineered coatings) to induce a Cr-rich, dual-phase passive layer with gradient composition and enhanced hardness at the top surface.
decision.why: Given the observed benefits of Cr in forming protective oxide layers in Cr-containing HEAs like AlCoCrFeNi and the trend in improving bulk performance via composition and processing modifications, engineering the surface offers a targeted solution. This approach directly addresses the need for a robust interface that can concurrently mitigate wear and corrosion at high temperatures, making it the most plausible next step following prior work.

families.principle: Tailoring the elemental makeup governs the formation of stable, protective oxide films and phase stability essential for resisting high‐temperature tribo-corrosion.
cues_for: high-entropy alloy (HEA) with multiple principal elements
cues_against: There is little indication that simply altering processing or surface treatments alone would directly overcome the intrinsic degradation issues.
families.best_lever: Optimizing the HEA composition—specifically balancing Cr, Al, and other elements—to promote the formation of a continuous, protective oxide passivation layer that resists both wear and corrosion at elevated temperatures.

families.principle: Surface modifications, including coatings or engineered oxide layers, directly protect the material from wear and corrosive attack by modifying interface properties.
cues_against: the context emphasizes the inherent advantages of HEA bulk composition over secondary surface treatments
families.best_lever: Develop an engineered surface—via techniques such as laser surface melting or deposition of a tailored oxide coating—that enhances the passive film formation on the HEA, thereby augmenting its tribo-corrosion resistance.

families.principle: Heat treatments can drive phase transformations and relieve residual stresses, thereby enhancing the stability of protective phases under high-temperature conditions.
cues_for: inferential need to stabilize beneficial surface/passivating phases
cues_against: the focus on HEA composition suggests that intrinsic material design is the primary lever
families.best_lever: Implement an optimized annealing schedule that promotes the formation and stability of a protective oxide layer while refining the microstructure.

families.principle: Engineering the grain size and phase distribution affects mechanical properties and the ability to form a continuous passive film against tribo-corrosion.
cues_against: the description prioritizes material composition over microstructural tailoring
families.best_lever: Design a multi-phase microstructure with fine grain architecture that balances hardness (to resist wear) and corrosion passivity.

families.principle: The synthesis method influences microstructural homogeneity and defect density, which indirectly affects corrosion and wear resistance.
cues_for: accelerated degradation in extreme environments could be mitigated by avoiding deleterious phases
cues_against: the question emphasizes alloy design via composition rather than synthesis method adjustments
families.best_lever: Employ rapid solidification or other advanced synthesis techniques to ensure uniform elemental distribution and suppress undesirable phase segregation.
